processing: Mainly steamed sencha, with deep-steamed fukamushi increasingly common. Most first-flush leaf is shaded for about a week before picking in the kabuse manner.
harvest_season: First flush comes earlier than in Shizuoka, making this one of Japan's early-season areas. The northern hill zone around Nochidake is known for the higher grades.
appearance_dry: As with other sencha, fine dark-green needles, shorter and more broken in deep-steamed lots.
appearance_liquor: A clear young green, with more depth and some cloud when deep-steamed.
appearance_wet: Soft bright green leaf, finer and more broken in fukamushi.
taste_profile: A fresh, clean aroma with a rich sweetness; Yutakamidori fukamushi is dense and full, while Saemidori is sweet and savoury with little astringency.

brewing.notes: Fukamushi needs a shorter first steep, around 40 seconds, and a fine-mesh pot, as its small particles cloud the cup and clog a coarse filter.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's crop, and new tea reaches the market earlier than Shizuoka's. Since April 2017 the name also covers Ei and Kawanabe tea from Minamikyushu, so it is a wide label now: look for the cultivar, the steaming style and the district.
description:
Chiran tea is the green tea of Minamikyushu in Kagoshima, the largest tea-growing municipality in Japan, with about 3,425 hectares and some 13,000 tonnes of crude tea a year. Kagoshima, led by this area, passed Shizuoka in the 2024 crop to rank first in Japan for the first time since prefectural statistics began in 1959.

Volcanic shirasu and dark ash soils here are acid and free-draining, which tea likes and many crops do not. Most first-flush leaf gets about a week of shade before picking. Hill plots around Nochidake lean to fine tea, while the southern districts run large machine-picked fields.

The cup is a clear young green with a fresh scent. Four cultivars cover about 80% of the fields. Yutakamidori makes the dense deep-steamed style, Yabukita is balanced, Saemidori is sweet and bright, and scarce Asatsuyu is rich enough to be called natural gyokuro.

Choosing by cultivar tells you more than the name. A single-cultivar Saemidori or Asatsuyu shows what the area can do; a blended fukamushi is a solid daily cup.
history:
A local tradition, marked by a monument at Temino Pass, credits Heike refugees with starting tea in the hills in the Kamakura period. Serious growing began in 1872, when villagers cleared land released from the Sata-Shimazu family, and a growers' association brought in technicians and Uji methods.

Machinery arrived from 1920, and a prefectural branch tea station followed in 1930. A black tea factory was set up in 1934 with prefectural backing, and in 1938 black tea made here was presented for the emperor.

Import liberalisation in the 1960s undercut the black tea, and farmers moved to green. In 2017 the Ei and Kawanabe names merged into Chiran-cha.
